analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to cover mental health care on the same terms as physical care.
analysis.headline: A mental health insurance parity bill backed by 249 House cosponsors — including 46 Republicans — died in committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced employer group health plans that cover mental illness to apply the same copays, deductibles, visit limits, and annual caps to mental health care as they do to medical and surgical care — unless the limits were equally strict for both. It did not force any plan to add mental health coverage, exempted employers with 50 or fewer workers, and let insurers keep managing mental health care. It also ordered a study of what the rule costs and of extending it to addiction treatment.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of insured workers and their families who need mental health treatment. Under the bill, a plan could no longer charge a $50 mental health copay while charging $15 for a doctor visit, or cap therapy visits at 20 a year while allowing unlimited physical therapy visits, unless it applied the same rules to physical care. People with depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and other DSM-listed conditions would get coverage closer to what they get for a broken bone or cancer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured workers needing mental health care

how_it_helps.text: Group health plans could not impose treatment limits or cost-sharing on mental health benefits unless the same limits applied to medical and surgical benefits, covering deductibles, coinsurance, copays, and annual and lifetime limits.

The bill covers all categories of mental health conditions listed in the DSM-IV, and applies to both self-insured employer plans under ERISA and insured group plans under the Public Health Service Act.
It does not raise state standards: state laws with stronger protections are not preempted, so states could still go further.

The bill was designed to ease cost concerns: plans are not required to offer mental health benefits at all, small employers with 2 to 50 employees are exempt, and a GAO study was required on the effects on insurance costs, access, and quality.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and the health insurers who administer their plans. Equalizing mental health benefits means paying for more therapy visits, psychiatric care, and medication coverage at standard cost-sharing, which the bill's sponsors anticipated would raise premiums somewhat — which is why the bill ordered a federal study of the cost effects. Part of that cost would likely reach workers through premium contributions, though families who currently pay far more for mental health care would come out ahead.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require any plan to offer mental health benefits in the first place; a plan that covers only medical and surgical care does not have to add mental health coverage.
Substance abuse and chemical dependency treatment are explicitly excluded from the parity requirement, so addiction coverage would remain unequal.
Employers with 2 to 50 employees are exempt, so many workers at small businesses would not benefit.
Plans only have to provide parity for in-network mental health care; out-of-network coverage can remain more restricted, as long as in-network providers are reasonably available.
Insurers may continue to medically manage mental health benefits through preauthorization and utilization review, so some gatekeeping remains.

Equalizing benefits raises costs for employers and insurers, and some of that would likely be passed to workers through premiums — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge, which is why the bill orders a GAO study of the effects on insurance costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades modestly higher premiums for a large, concrete gain: equal treatment for mental illness in employer coverage, which in 2003 routinely carried higher copays, fewer visits, and annual caps that physical care did not. Its carve-outs — no mandate to offer coverage, a small-employer exemption, an exclusion for addiction treatment, and weaker out-of-network rules — are real limitations, and they reflect compromises made to reduce cost objections. But for the workers who need mental health care, the core change is substantial. The bill was narrow and carefully built to address the objections raised when a similar Senate bill passed in 1996, which makes its quiet death harder to explain on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees, then parked in subcommittees, and neither ever acted on it — no hearing produced a bill, no markup was held, and the House never voted before the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 27, 2003, with 135 original cosponsors from both parties.
It accumulated 249 cosponsors — 202 Democrats, 46 Republicans, and 1 Independent — well over a majority of the House.
It was referred to the Education and Workforce Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to the Health Subcommittee and the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health insurers who would have borne the cost of equalizing mental health benefits are better off because the bill died. The 249 cosponsors never had to cast a recorded vote, and workers with mental health conditions kept the unequal coverage the bill would have ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan on paper — 249 cosponsors split roughly 202 Democrats, 46 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but the bill never reached a vote, so the record shows no division on the merits.

industries.note: The bill would have barred plans from imposing stricter cost-sharing and visit limits on mental health care than on physical care, ending a practice that saved insurers money at the expense of people seeking treatment. Insurers could still manage care through preauthorization, and out-of-network parity was not required.

Employers sponsoring group plans would have absorbed higher benefit costs or passed them to workers through premiums. Many large employers already offered some mental health coverage, so the change is real but not uniformly costly.
Therapists, psychologists, and psychiatrists would see demand rise as visit caps and higher cost-sharing were lifted, and patients would find care more affordable.
